new_entities.name: Maternal omega-3 supplementation during pregnancy
new_entities.description: Supplemental omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids, usually DHA with or without EPA, taken during pregnancy.

new_entities.name: Child cognitive function
new_entities.description: Cognitive, language, executive, and related developmental performance in childhood.

edges.effect_quant: Across randomized trials, prenatal omega-3 supplementation has not shown a robust, consistent lift in child cognition, although some follow-up studies report small advantages in selected domains or subgroups.
edges.population: children born to mothers supplemented with omega-3 fatty acids during pregnancy
edges.mechanism: DHA is a structural lipid in the developing fetal brain and retina, so a cognitive benefit is biologically plausible if maternal intake is limiting. The inconsistency in trials suggests that baseline nutrition, dose, timing, and social environment matter more than a universal treatment effect.
edges.summary: The most useful summary is that prenatal omega-3 supplementation remains biologically appealing but empirically modest for cognition. The early RCT meta-analysis found no consistent overall cognitive gain, the larger Cochrane review reported very few longer-term child differences, and a careful U.S. follow-up trial found only scattered benefits that disappeared after stronger adjustment.
edges.caveats: This edge is about cognition, not the better-supported preterm-birth outcomes of prenatal omega-3. Trial populations, doses, and developmental tests vary a lot, so null or weak results do not prove there is never benefit, only that the average cognitive payoff has been hard to show reliably.

evidence.citation: GouldJF et al 2013 Am J Clin Nutr
evidence.notes: The effect of maternal omega-3 (n-3) LCPUFA supplementation during pregnancy on early childhood cognitive and visual development: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
